resources.string: This section demonstrates various techniques that applications can use to collect your data without your explicit consent. Each demo provides a real-world example of how this \'sneaky\' data collection can impact your privacy.

Device fingerprinting is a powerful technique used to identify and track you, even if you try to hide. This section breaks down different fingerprinting methods, explaining how they work and what the consequences are for your digital anonymity.
Stealing location data from image metadata.
Pinpointing your location using nearby Wi-Fi networks.
Reading sensitive information you copy to the clipboard.
Identifying your device based on its unique characteristics.
Using sensor data to create a unique device fingerprint.

Many digital cameras and smartphones record metadata in image files, including the GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken. This demo shows how an app can access this EXIF data and extract your location without you ever explicitly sharing it.

Even with GPS turned off, your phone is constantly scanning for Wi-Fi networks. The names (SSIDs) of these networks can be used to determine your precise location by cross-referencing them with public databases of Wi-Fi access points and their locations.

When you copy text, images, or files, they are stored in the system clipboard. This demo shows how easily an app can access the clipboard content in the background, potentially stealing passwords, credit card numbers, or other private information.

Your device has a unique combination of hardware and software attributes, such as screen resolution, installed fonts, and user agent string. This demo shows how these attributes can be combined to create a unique fingerprint that can be used to track you across different apps and websites.

Slight imperfections in your device\'s accelerometer, gyroscope, and magnetometer can be used to create a unique fingerprint. This demo shows how an app can read this sensor data and use it to identify your device.
A social media app could track your location history by analyzing the photos you upload.
A malicious app could use this data to build a profile of your daily routine.
Retail stores can track your movements within the store to analyze shopping habits.
An app could identify your home and work locations based on the Wi-Fi networks you connect to most often.
A malicious keyboard app could steal your passwords as you copy and paste them.
An e-commerce app could read a tracking number you copied to suggest related products.
Advertisers can use device fingerprinting to track your browsing habits even if you clear your cookies.
A website could use your device fingerprint to link your current session to a previous one, even if you are not logged in.
A website could use sensor data to detect if you are the same user who visited before, even if you are using a different browser or VPN.
A malicious app could use this data to track your movements and activities.

Apps on your phone are constantly tracking you - collecting your location, browsing habits, and personal information.\n\nSpyCheck reveals this hidden surveillance in real-time, showing you exactly when and how apps spy on you.

SpyCheck monitors your phone's internet traffic.

When an app tries to send your data to tracking companies like Google Analytics, Facebook, or data brokers, you'll see a pop-up warning.

This happens invisibly with normal apps - SpyCheck makes it visible!

To show you real-time tracking, SpyCheck needs the same dangerous permissions that tracking apps use:

• VPN Access - to see internet traffic
• Usage Stats - to identify apps
• Display Overlay - to show warnings

IMPORTANT: These are educational demos. When you're done, REVOKE these permissions!

Here's what to do:

1. Grant the 3 permissions
2. Tap "Start Watching"
3. Minimize the app
4. Use your phone normally
5. Watch the tracking warnings appear!

Apps can extract GPS coordinates from your photos without needing Location permission. Every photo taken with your phone\'s camera may contain EXIF metadata including exact GPS coordinates showing where it was taken. This means an app with only Photos permission can track everywhere you\'ve been.
Dating apps accessing location history through photo metadata
Social media apps building location profiles without explicit permission
Photo editing apps harvesting user movement patterns
Apps can extract your exact location from photos without needing Location permission. Every photo taken with your phone\'s camera may contain GPS coordinates showing exactly where it was taken.

Any app with Photos permission can see where every picture was taken — even without Location permission. This creates a complete tracking profile of everywhere you go.
